title: Fallacies and Pitfalls
summary: Calculate end-to-end pipeline speedup using Amdahl's law when optimizing an isolated ML component.

blocks.md:
This lesson follows **Fallacies and Pitfalls** in *System Paradigms* (Vol I). By the end you should be able to:

- Calculate end-to-end pipeline speedup using Amdahl's law when optimizing an isolated ML component
- Explain why hardware-aware compilation and kernel fusion are essential for efficient edge deployment
- Evaluate the pitfall of ignoring operational expenses and DevOps labor when calculating edge ML deployment costs
- Explain the physical and statistical limits that prevent data quantity from guaranteeing deployment accuracy gains
- Explain how kernel fusion reduces memory traffic and kernel launch overhead in inference pipelines

blocks.source: Vol I, System Paradigms, § Fallacies and Pitfalls
blocks.md: Most deployment misconceptions share one root. Each treats a physical envelope as a software detail that a later optimization can fix. Data movement, thermal dissipation, and hardware balance can invalidate otherwise reasonable optimization choices, and each fallacy and pitfall below records a system mismatched to its operating envelope.

blocks.title: Map of the section
blocks.md:
The section is organised as:

- Summary

Pay attention to: Amdahl's law applied to ML pipelines and end-to-end system speedup limits; Per-target binary compilation and kernel fusion vs. generic model artifacts; Total Cost of Ownership fallacies and training data scaling limitations.

blocks.prompt: Think first: Why does choosing an on-premises edge deployment solely because its hardware amortizes to a lower monthly compute cost than a cloud VM often result in a higher Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)?
blocks.md: Hardware compute cost is only one fraction of the total cost of ownership. Deploying on-premise edge fleets introduces substantial recurring operational expenses (OpEx), including distributed network engineering, on-site hardware maintenance, security patching, and DevOps reliability engineering, alongside extended development timelines. Adding these costs can erase an apparent hardware-only saving. A valid total-cost verdict requires the cloud and edge budgets to include comparable operating costs, capacity, availability, and accounting periods; the chapter's cloud-compute-only figure does not supply that matched comparison.

questions.q: A smartphone camera pipeline takes 200 ms total: 100 ms for the image signal processor (ISP), 60 ms for ML scene classification, and 40 ms for postprocessing. If an engineering team optimizes the ML model to run \$10× faster (reducing ML time from 60 ms to 6 ms), what is the overall system-level speedup?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. Prior to optimization, total latency is \$100 ms + 60 ms + 40 ms = 200 ms. The ML model represents p = frac60200 = 0.30 (30%) of total pipeline execution time. Optimizing the ML stage by s = 10× reduces its latency to frac6010 = 6 ms, resulting in a new total latency of \$100 ms + 6 ms + 40 ms = 146 ms. The overall system speedup is frac200 ms146 ms approx 1.37×. Even an infinite ML speedup (s = infty) would yield at most frac200140 approx 1.43× speedup because the remaining 70% of the pipeline is unoptimized. The option claiming a \$10.00× system speedup commits the classic fallacy of assuming model-level speedup translates linearly to end-to-end system speedup. The options claiming \$5.50× or \$0.73× represent calculation errors.

questions.q: Why does deploying a single generic FP32 model binary across diverse edge devices (e.g., Arm CPU, Apple Neural Engine, and Google Coral Edge TPU) result in suboptimal efficiency compared to per-target compilation?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C. Different edge accelerators feature unique hardware architectures, such as specialized INT8 tensor systolic arrays, proprietary NPU delegates, and distinct on-chip memory hierarchies. A generic model binary fails to utilize kernel fusion (which avoids round-trip memory traffic between layers), cannot map operations to dedicated low-precision datapaths, and fails to align tensor dimensions with on-chip cache lines. The options claiming PCI Express signature violations, undefined mobile float math, or automatic OS weight deletion are entirely fabricated.
questions.hint: Think about: explain why hardware-aware compilation and kernel fusion are essential for efficient edge deployment.
options: Generic model binaries violate cryptographic signatures required by PCI Express buses.
Floating-point operations are mathematically undefined on mobile CPUs.
Generic binaries cannot exploit hardware-specific kernel fusion, dedicated fixed-point INT8 matrix datapaths, or accelerator-specific on-chip SRAM memory tiling.
The operating system automatically deletes untuned model weights to prevent memory fragmentation.

questions.q: Increasing the quantity of training data is guaranteed to continuously improve deployed model performance regardless of model capacity, label noise, or domain distribution shift.
questions.explanation: False. Data scaling benefits are bounded by three critical constraints: model capacity (a small model saturates and cannot absorb more information), data quality (noisy, mislabeled, or redundant data harms accuracy), and distribution alignment (adding massive out-of-domain data does not improve, and can degrade, performance on target deployment distributions).
questions.hint: Think about: explain the physical and statistical limits that prevent data quantity from guaranteeing deployment accuracy gains.

blocks.prompt: Explain it: What is kernel fusion in ML compilers, and how does it optimize memory-bound inference pipelines?
blocks.md: Kernel fusion is an optimization technique where a compiler merges multiple adjacent operations in a neural network graph (such as Conv2D, BatchNorm, and ReLU) into a single executed kernel. By computing intermediate values directly in high-speed processor registers or on-chip SRAM rather than writing them back to off-chip DRAM and reading them again for the next layer, kernel fusion drastically reduces off-chip memory traffic ($D_{\text{vol}}/\text{BW}$) and kernel launch overhead ($L_{\text{lat}}$).

You can now explain why hardware-aware compilation and kernel fusion are essential for efficient edge deployment.
You can now evaluate the pitfall of ignoring operational expenses and DevOps labor when calculating edge ML deployment costs.
You can now explain the physical and statistical limits that prevent data quantity from guaranteeing deployment accuracy gains.
